q: On a position-versus-time graph, what does the slope of the line represent?
e: Change in position divided by change in time is velocity.

q: On a velocity-versus-time graph, what does the slope of the line represent?
e: Change in velocity divided by change in time is acceleration.

q: On a velocity-versus-time graph, what does the area between the line and the time axis represent?
e: Velocity times time gives displacement.

q: What does a horizontal line on a position-versus-time graph show?
e: The position does not change.

q: A velocity-versus-time graph shows a straight line sloping upward from the origin. What kind of motion is this?
e: Velocity increases steadily.

q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
e: A vector has both magnitude and direction.

q: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
e: A scalar has magnitude only.

q: A 3 N force acts east and a 4 N force acts north on an object. What is the magnitude of the net force?
A 6 N force acts east and a 2 N force acts west on an object. What is the net force?
e: Subtract opposite forces.

q: A runner completes one lap around a 400 m track and returns to the start. What is the runner's displacement?
e: Displacement compares the final position with the starting position.

q: A cyclist travels 100 m in 20 s at a constant speed. What is the speed?
e: Speed = distance ÷ time.

q: A car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
e: a = Δv ÷ t.

q: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. How far does it travel?
Ignoring air resistance, about how fast is an object falling after 3 s of free fall from rest? (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²)
e: v = gt.

q: A person walks 3 m east and then 3 m west. What is the total distance traveled?
e: Distance adds up all of the path length.

q: In uniform circular motion, in which direction does the acceleration point?
o: toward the center of the circle
e: Centripetal acceleration points inward.

q: An object moves at 4 m/s on a circle of radius 2 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
Ignoring air resistance, what happens to the horizontal velocity of a horizontally launched projectile?
e: No horizontal force acts on it.

q: One ball is dropped and another is launched horizontally from the same height at the same moment. Ignoring air resistance, which lands first?
o: they land at the same time
e: Vertical motion is identical for both.

q: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. Why is it accelerating?
o: its direction of velocity keeps changing
e: Velocity is a vector, and its direction changes.

q: According to Newton's first law, what happens to a moving object with no net force on it?
o: it continues moving at constant velocity
e: Objects keep their motion unless acted on by a net force.

q: What is inertia?
o: the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion
e: More mass means more inertia.

q: Which quantity is a measure of an object's inertia?
e: Greater mass resists change in motion more.

q: A passenger lurches forward when a car brakes suddenly. Which idea explains this?
e: The body tends to keep moving.

q: What is true about the net force on an object in equilibrium?
e: Forces balance.

q: What is the net force on a 10 kg object accelerating at 3 m/s²?
e: F = ma.

q: What is the weight of a 5 kg object near Earth's surface? (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²)
e: W = mg.

q: A 20 N force pushes a box right and a 5 N friction force pushes left. What is the net force?
e: Subtract the opposing force.

q: Which force acts perpendicular to a surface and supports an object resting on it?
e: It pushes away from the surface.

q: Which force keeps a car moving in a circle on a flat curve?
o: a force pointing away from the center
friction between the tires and the road, acting as a centripetal force
e: A center-directed force is needed.

q: According to Newton's third law, forces between two objects are what?
o: equal and in the same direction
equal in size and opposite in direction
e: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

q: A rocket moves forward when it pushes exhaust gas backward. Which law explains this?
o: the law of conservation of charge
e: The gas pushes the rocket in return.

q: When you push on a wall, what does the wall do?
o: pushes back with an equal force
pushes back with a smaller force
e: Action-reaction forces are equal.

q: Why don't the action and reaction forces cancel each other out?
o: they act in the same direction
e: A net force requires forces on the same object.

q: If the distance between two masses doubles, what happens to the gravitational force between them?
e: Gravity follows an inverse square law.

q: If one of two masses doubles, what happens to the gravitational force between them?
e: Force is proportional to each mass.

q: What is the approximate value of the universal gravitational constant G?
e: A very small number, so gravity is weak between everyday objects.

q: If both masses and the distance between them are all doubled, what happens to the gravitational force?
e: Masses give a factor of 4 and distance gives a factor of 1/4.

q: If the distance between two charges doubles, what happens to the electric force between them?
e: The electric force also follows an inverse square law.

q: How do two objects with opposite charges interact?
o: they have no force between them
e: Opposite charges attract.

q: If one charge triples while the other charge and distance stay the same, what happens to the electric force?
o: it is nine times as large
e: Force is proportional to each charge.

q: The Coulomb constant k is about 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is this number in standard form?
e: 10⁹ means 9 followed by 9 zeros.

q: What does an electric generator do?
o: converts mechanical energy into electrical energy using a magnetic field
converts electrical energy into heat only
e: A coil spins in a magnetic field.

q: What does an electric motor do?
o: converts electrical energy into mechanical energy using magnetic forces
e: Current in a magnetic field experiences a force.

q: Why does the needle of a compass point north?
o: it aligns with Earth's magnetic field
it is attracted by the Moon
e: Earth acts like a giant magnet.

q: Which everyday device uses electromagnets to lift scrap metal?
e: Current through a coil creates a magnetic field that can be switched on and off.

q: A balloon rubbed on hair becomes negative and the hair becomes positive. What does this show?
o: electrons moved from the hair to the balloon
e: Electrons are transferred and total charge stays the same.

q: Charging by conduction requires what?
o: direct contact between a charged object and a neutral object
e: Charge flows during contact.

q: Charging by induction results in a final charge on the neutral object that is what?
o: opposite to the charged object that was brought near
the same as the charged object
e: Charges rearrange and then the object is grounded.

q: What does the law of conservation of charge say?
o: the total charge in an isolated system stays the same
charge can be created from nothing
e: Charge is transferred, not created or destroyed.

q: In a series circuit, how many paths are there for current?
o: as many as there are bulbs
e: All components are connected in a single loop.

q: In a series circuit, what happens if one bulb burns out?
e: The circuit is broken.

q: In a parallel circuit, what is the same across each branch?
e: Each branch connects to the same two points.

q: Two resistors of 2 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
e: Resistances add in series.

q: Two identical 6 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
e: Equal resistors in parallel divide the resistance by the number of resistors.

q: Why are household outlets wired in parallel?
o: so that all devices turn off together
each device gets the full voltage and works independently
e: One device can be off while others stay on.

q: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor. What is the current?
e: I = V ÷ R.

q: A device carries 2 A at 10 V. How much power does it use?
e: P = IV.

q: A circuit has 9 V and 3 A. What is the resistance?
e: R = V ÷ I.

q: What is the unit of electric power?
e: One watt is one joule per second.

q: If the voltage across a fixed resistor doubles, what happens to the current?
e: Current is proportional to voltage.

q: How much work does a 10 N force do pushing a box 5 m in the direction of the force?
e: W = Fd.

q: A person holds a heavy box without moving it. How much work is done on the box?
o: none, because there is no displacement
a lot, because the force is large
e: Work needs displacement in the direction of the force.

q: A machine does 100 J of work in 5 s. What is its power?
e: P = W ÷ t.

q: A waiter carries a tray at constant speed across a flat room. Does the waiter's upward force on the tray do work?
o: No, because the force is perpendicular to the motion
Yes, because there is a force
Yes, because the tray has weight
e: Work depends on the component of force along the motion.

q: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s?
e: KE = ½mv².

q: What is the gravitational potential energy of a 2 kg object at a height of 10 m? (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²)
e: PE = mgh.

q: If a car's speed doubles, its kinetic energy is multiplied by what factor?
e: Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared.

q: Mechanical energy of a system is the sum of what?
e: ME = KE + PE.

q: A ball falls from a shelf. What happens to its energy as it falls?
o: kinetic energy changes into potential energy
gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy
e: Total mechanical energy stays about the same without friction.

q: On a roller coaster without friction, where is the kinetic energy greatest?
o: at the start of the climb only
e: The speed is greatest at the bottom.

q: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object equals what?
e: W = ΔKE.

q: When a sliding box stops because of friction, where does its kinetic energy go?
e: Friction transforms motion energy into heat.

q: A ball dropped from 5 m has about what speed just before it hits the ground? (g ≈ 9.8 m/s², ignore air)
What is the momentum of a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s?
e: p = mv.

q: Impulse is equal to what?
e: J = FΔt = Δp.

q: How does an airbag reduce injury in a collision?
o: it increases the time over which the person stops, reducing the force
it increases the force on the person
it makes the car go faster
e: The same change in momentum over a longer time means less force.

q: Why do crumple zones on cars help protect passengers?
o: they lengthen the stopping time, reducing the average force
e: Impulse is the same but force is smaller.

q: In an inelastic collision, what happens to the total kinetic energy?
o: some is converted to other forms such as heat
e: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.

q: In a perfectly elastic collision, what is conserved?
e: No kinetic energy is lost.

q: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg cart at rest, and they stick together. What is their speed afterward?
e: 6 kg·m/s ÷ 3 kg.

q: A gun fires a bullet forward and recoils backward. Which principle explains the recoil?
e: Total momentum starts at zero and stays at zero.

q: On what does the period of a simple pendulum mainly depend (for small angles)?
o: how far it started from the middle only
e: Longer pendulums swing more slowly.

q: A wave has a period of 0.5 s. What is its frequency?
A mass on a spring moves fastest at what point?
o: the top of the motion only
e: All of the energy is kinetic at equilibrium.

q: What kind of force acts on an object in simple harmonic motion?
o: a restoring force toward the equilibrium position
a force away from the center
a constant force in one direction
e: The force is proportional to displacement.

q: What does a wave transfer from one place to another?
e: The medium vibrates but does not travel with the wave.

q: Which of these waves is longitudinal?
e: Sound consists of compressions and rarefactions.

q: In a transverse wave, how does the medium vibrate?
o: perpendicular to the direction the wave travels
parallel to the direction the wave travels
e: Like a wave on a rope.

q: Which type of wave can travel through a vacuum?
e: They do not need a medium.

q: What are the regions of high pressure in a sound wave called?
e: Particles are pushed close together.

q: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed?
e: v = fλ.

q: What property of a sound wave determines how loud it is?
e: Greater amplitude carries more energy.

q: What property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
e: Higher frequency sounds higher.

q: A wave's speed stays the same while its frequency doubles. What happens to the wavelength?
e: v = fλ.

q: What is it called when a wave bounces off a surface?
e: The law of reflection applies.

q: What causes refraction?
o: a change in wave speed when entering a different medium
e: The wave bends as its speed changes.

q: What is diffraction?
o: the bending of waves around obstacles or through openings
e: It is strongest when the opening is similar in size to the wavelength.

q: When two waves overlap and make a larger amplitude, this is called what?
e: Crests align with crests.

q: An ambulance siren sounds higher in pitch as it approaches. This is called what?
e: The waves are compressed in front of the moving source.

q: Radio telescopes detect what kind of waves from space?
e: Large dishes collect radio signals.

q: Which electromagnetic waves are used to cook food in a microwave oven?
e: They make water molecules vibrate.

q: Which electromagnetic waves are used for medical imaging of bones?
e: They pass through soft tissue more easily than bone.

q: Night-vision devices detect which type of electromagnetic radiation?
e: Warm objects emit infrared.

q: Why does each element have a unique emission spectrum?
o: its electrons have a unique set of energy levels
e: Each atom emits only certain wavelengths.

q: How is a photon emitted by an atom?
o: an electron drops to a lower energy level
an electron moves to a higher energy level
e: The energy difference is released as light.

q: How do astronomers learn what elements a star contains?
o: by analyzing the spectrum of its light
e: The spectral lines match known elements.

q: What kind of image does a plane mirror form?
o: a virtual image, the same size as the object, behind the mirror
e: The image appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

q: What does the law of reflection state?
o: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
the angle of incidence is twice the reflection angle
e: Both angles are measured from the normal.

q: Light entering glass from air slows down. How does it bend?
e: Light bends toward the normal in a slower medium.

q: What does a converging (convex) lens do to parallel light rays?
o: bends them toward a focal point
e: It focuses light.

q: Why does light stay inside an optical fiber?
o: total internal reflection at the walls
e: Light hits the boundary at angles greater than the critical angle.

q: In the photoelectric effect, electrons are ejected from a metal only if the light has what?
e: Photon energy must exceed the work function.

q: Increasing the brightness of light below the threshold frequency has what effect on the photoelectric effect?
o: electrons are ejected only at first
e: Each photon must carry enough energy on its own.

q: Which model of light explains the photoelectric effect?
o: light as a continuous wave only
light as photons with energy E = hf
e: Einstein proposed light comes in quanta.

q: Emission spectra show only specific wavelengths. What does this indicate about atomic energy levels?
e: Only certain energy differences are possible.

q: What does the polarization of light show about its nature?
e: Only transverse waves can be polarized.

q: Two polarizing filters are crossed at 90°. How much light passes through both?
Light of intensity 100 passes through a polarizer whose axis is 30° from the light's polarization. By Malus's law, about what intensity passes?
Why do polarized sunglasses reduce glare?
o: they change the color of light
they block horizontally polarized reflected light
e: Reflected glare is mostly polarized.

q: How do 3-D movie glasses create separate images for each eye?
o: each lens polarizes light in a different direction
e: Two differently polarized images are shown on the screen.

q: What is wave-particle duality?
o: matter and light show both wave and particle behavior
e: The behavior depends on the experiment.

q: Electrons sent through two slits form an interference pattern. What does this show?
o: electrons are not particles at all
e: A wave-like pattern builds up from individual electrons.

q: What does superposition of quantum states mean?
o: a system can only be in one state
a system is always at rest
a system can exist in a combination of states until measured
e: Measurement gives one outcome.

q: What is a photon?
e: Its energy depends on frequency.

q: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle says that you cannot do what?
o: know the exact position and momentum of a particle at the same time
e: There is a limit to how precisely both can be known.

q: What do quantum computers use in place of ordinary bits?
o: qubits that can be in superposition
e: A qubit can be in a combination of 0 and 1.

q: Which everyday devices rely on quantum mechanics?
e: Their operation depends on quantized energy levels.

q: What principle allows an electron microscope to see very small objects?
o: electrons have wave properties with very short wavelengths
e: Shorter wavelength gives better resolution.
